findings: The `User` interface declares `phone: string` (required, non-null) but the `users` table defines `phone TEXT NULL`; `listActiveUsers` does `SELECT id, email, phone FROM users` and casts the raw rows straight to `User[]` with no null-check or validation layer, so any row with a NULL phone silently violates the TS contract at runtime — code trusting `user.phone` as a string (e.g. calling string methods on it) will crash or misbehave, and this stays invisible in staging until a row with a null phone (e.g. a legacy user, or one from before phone was collected) is hit.

`listActiveUsers` has no WHERE clause at all (`SELECT id, email, phone FROM users`) despite its name, so it returns soft-deleted users (`deleted_at` set) as if they were active — the `deleted_at` column exists specifically to support soft deletion but is never referenced anywhere in this file, so every caller of this function is silently working with a wrong active-user set.

The signup duplicate-email check (`SELECT id FROM users WHERE email=$1`) also ignores `deleted_at`, so once a user is soft-deleted their email is still reported as taken (`existing.length` > 0) — a different person (or the original user) can never reuse that email address, a direct, concrete consequence of the same missing deleted_at filtering that breaks listActiveUsers.

Email uniqueness is enforced only in application code via a check-then-insert pattern (`SELECT ... WHERE email=$1` followed by a separate `INSERT`), with no transaction or locking, and the schema explicitly has no UNIQUE constraint on email (per the schema.sql comment) — two concurrent signup calls with the same email can both pass the existence check before either INSERT completes, producing duplicate email rows that nothing in the DB or code prevents.
